before: Part of building who you are is untangling yourself from whatever pulls you away from your own knowing in return for belonging, like a political tribe or another group you identify with which expects consistent positions and predictable reactions. Or the expectations of a family or religion that’s kind to you. Going along with those might just feel like being good. Most groups expect some conformity, which is ordinary, like your family wanting a particular kind of son or daughter, or your friends’ rules about what you can joke about or get upset about. But if going along means betraying yourself, that’s the bargain.
after: Beauty, intelligence, achievement and caretaking can all be real gifts, but they become belonging bargains when failing in the arena feels like losing yourself. Your little one, with nobody parenting it, takes those bargains to survive, because belonging feels like life or death (and when you're small, it more or less is). That happens to children of good parents too, and it isn't a flaw in you. Noticing where you're betraying yourself to belong, and keeping your own ground, is called self-differentiation. It also means noticing when praise or pity suddenly changes what you think you know, or fear or attraction does, and resonance can too.

guide_passage:
The r4 guide's passage (the passage this carries):
When value isn’t felt internally, a person can become a “human doer”: worth has to be earned in an external arena. It may be beauty, athleticism, or sexual desirability; intelligence and grades; money, status, or a sophisticated spiritual identity; or becoming indispensable to everybody else’s problems. In its controlling form, caretaking can drift into keeping other people dependent, because being needed has become the caretaker’s main source of value.
brief:
- when value isn't felt inside, a person can become a "human doer": worth has to be earned in an outside arena
- the arenas the guide names, all four: beauty, athleticism or sexual desirability; intelligence and grades; money, status or a sophisticated spiritual identity; becoming indispensable to everybody else's problems
- in its controlling form, caretaking can drift into keeping other people dependent, because being needed has become the caretaker's main source of value (keep "can", "in its controlling form" and "drift": not every caretaker does this)
- context, not for the text: the paragraph before ends on where going along turns into the bargain, betraying yourself. This one turns to a second kind of bargain, worth you have to earn, and a reader should see that turn in its first words. The next paragraph says these can be real gifts and when they become bargains, so that isn't said here
length: three to five sentences, 70 to 110 words
